Some people seem very nervous as they don't want to be left in the dark and can't do what they need to. They are comfortable with Windows and have been for quite some time. Linux is just different than Windows. The average person can do whatever they need to on Linux. Sure there are some exceptions. Gamers and people who use proprietary software for work thats only available on Windows will have some difficulties. For regular folks who just browse the internet, do some document editing, and other basic things I think Linux is perfect. There's even tools for image, video and sound editing if thats what you're into, and most of it is free.

At this point, I can't justify the cost of Microsoft products considering how capable and easy to use the free and open source alternatives are. After converting my parents (who had no experience with computers outside of Windows) to Ubuntu a few years ago, and converting my SO to Linux Mint, I have had no problems. The only time I've had to "fix" my parent's computer since installing Ubuntu has been to install a printer....and they didn't know how to do that on Windows either.

So if you are remotely curious about switching to Linux, I say try it out! There's a bunch of distros and many desktop environments. Boot to a live disk and test drive it before installing it on your hard drive. If you decide to take the plunge and install it to your hard drive, make sure you copy all your files onto another drive and verify they copied correctly before installing Linux over Windows. Even if you're going to try and dual boot Linux and Windows, back up your files from Windows to another drive before starting the process.

Good luck!
I see a lot of people asking about switching to Linux. Here's some words from someone who has and helped others along the way.

My advice to the newbies: don't let anyone convince you to go with arch or gentoo. These are not friendly systems. They are suitable for people who have experience with linux, the command lines, ... People will say "It's the best way to learn!" but do not fall for that. It might be the "purest" way to learn linux, but requires a lot of dedication and it'll take days/weeks before you have a system where you can actually do work/entertainment on.

I've seen so much people get recommended "Try Arch!" and they'll nope out minutes after the installation because it's so cumbersome to get it going, and then they go back to windows.
I completely agree with you. Very few people suggest learning to drive a car by first having to build one from scratch.

I think in total we all need to decide one one flavor to recommend. Throwing out 10 flavors just confuses people.

People if interested can explore arch and others. For the average user needs something simple and probably a ui that looks similar to windows.

While I agree with you on not starting off with Arch linux, an arch based distro can still be noob friendly. Manjaro and Antergos are some examples. I've started people of on just a vanilla install of Arch as well after showing them how to search for programs with on command. The people over at Manjaro have made a GUI front end for searching that is like synaptic as well.

Given the existence of the EvoLution installer, I'd say the comparison for vanilla arch is more like learning to drive a standard car vice an automatic. That being said, anyone who is not good with computers in general (elderly, handicapped, or non tech savvy) should not use vanilla arch.

I am not a fan of "the arch way" at all. I think that elitism is counter to the core ethos of Linux. I'm trying to get a friendly arch community off the ground over at /v(r)/positivearchlinux for anyone who's interested.
